title: Functionalized hydrogels of CeO 2 and Urolithin A synergistically scavenge ROS and activate mitophagy for cartilage repair

sections.abstract: In recent years, CeO 2 nanoparticles are promising biomaterials due to their excellent biocompatibility and antioxidant properties. This study utilizes a methacrylated gelatin (GelMA) hydrogel platform to construct a dual-functional composite material, CeUA@GelMA, by co-loading CeO 2 nanoparticles with urolithin A (UA). This material possesses both reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging and mitophagy activation capabilities, aiming to overcome the bottleneck in cartilage regeneration by regulating mitochondrial homeostasis. In vitro experiments confirmed that this material significantly reduces ROS levels within BMSCs under oxidative stress, maintains mitochondrial membrane potential, and promotes chondrogenic differentiation by upregulating genes such as Sox9, Col II, and ACAN. In vivo studies demonstrated that the CeUA@GelMA group achieved hyaline-like cartilage regeneration 8 weeks post-operation. The surface roughness of the newly formed cartilage was comparable to that of natural cartilage, with collagen and glycosaminoglycan density approaching normal cartilage levels. In summary, this research offers an innovative strategy and hydrogel material for cartilage tissue engineering through the regulation of mitochondrial homeostasis.
sections.introduction:
The repair of articular cartilage defects, one of the most challenging diseases in orthopaedics, is complicated by the unique biological properties of cartilage tissue [ 1 , 2 ]. Mature chondrocytes are embedded in a dense extracellular matrix that lacks vascularization and innervation, resulting in an extremely limited self-repair ability. Traditional treatments, such as microfracture surgery and autologous cartilage transplantation, can provide temporary symptom relief, but they often suffer from fibrosis of the repair tissue, insufficient mechanical properties, and long-term degeneration [ 3 ]. In recent years, the development of tissue engineering technology has provided new approaches for cartilage regeneration. However, maintaining the long-term homeostasis of chondrocytes in the defective region is still the core scientific challenge [ 4 , 5 ]. Studies have shown that chondrocyte mitochondrial dysfunction is a key pathological mechanism leading to degenerative changes. Under the influence of abnormal biomechanical stimulation and inflammatory microenvironment with the joint cavity, chondrocyte mitochondria produce excessive ROS, which triggers a cascade of oxidative stress [ 6 , 7 ]. This process not only directly damages mitochondrial DNA and respiratory chain complexes, but also accelerates the breakdown of type II collagen and proteoglycans by activating matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) through the NF-κB pathway [ 8 , 9 ]. It is worth noting that the accumulation of damaged mitochondria will create a vicious cycle - dysfunctional mitochondria will further release ROS, and the intracellular autophagy system is unable to effectively remove this mitochondrial garbage in a timely manner, which ultimately leads to apoptosis of chondrocytes and an imbalance in the metabolism of the extracellular matrix [ 10 , 11 ]. This finding suggests that the simultaneous regulation of ROS levels and promotion of mitophagy may be a revolutionary strategy to maintain cartilage homeostasis (see Scheme 1 ). Scheme 1 Schematic diagram of research design and experimental process. Scheme 1

Schematic diagram of research design and experimental process.

Current antioxidant therapies that modulate ROS mostly focus on single free radical scavenging, such as vitamin C and superoxide dismutase, but these have limited clinical translational effects [ 12 ]. The reason for this is that traditional antioxidants have problems such as short half-life and poor cell penetration. In recent years, CeO 2 nanoparticles have been increasingly widely used in the antioxidant field by virtue of their excellent bioavailability, antioxidant and targeting properties [ 13 , 14 ]. For example, Bin et al. used CeO 2 nanoparticles to scavenge excess ROS from neuronal cells to inhibit neuroinflammation [ 15 ]. Kong et al. used CeO 2 nanoparticles to efficiently scavenge excess ROS from oxidized human umbilical vein endothelial cells and simultaneously promote M2 macrophage polarization, thus regulating the modulation of inflammatory response [ 16 ]. Furthermore, dysfunction of mitophagy, a quality control system that selectively removes damaged mitochondria, is strongly associated with osteoarthritis progression. When the PINK1/Parkin signaling pathway is impaired, defective mitochondria cannot be effectively recognized and degraded by the autophagosome, leading to the continuous production of ROS and activation of NLRP3 inflammatory vesicles, resulting in the pathological triangle of oxidative stress-mitochondrial damage-inflammation amplification [ [17] , [18] , [19] ]. For example, Chen et al. developed a nanoparticle loaded with Urolithin A to promote mitophagy, which ultimately improved mitochondrial structure and inhibited iron death [ 20 ]. Jiang et al. accelerated diabetic wound healing in rats by utilizing Urolithin A to promote mitophagy in endothelial progenitor cells [ 21 ]. Therefore. The synergistic effects of CeO 2 nanoparticles and Urolithin A in scavenging ROS and promoting mitophagy are expected to improve the mitochondrial homeostasis of chondrocytes at the site of cartilage defects and accelerate cartilage repair.

Currently, hydrogel-based scaffolds for cartilage engineering are popular in the cartilage field. This is because hydrogels not only have similar structural and physicochemical properties to extracellular matrix to utilize cartilage development, but also have excellent slow-release properties that can be used for precise drug release. There are many types of hydrogels, such as DNA hydrogels, sodium alginate hydrogels, filipin hydrogels, and peptide hydrogels, etc., and different materials of hydrogels have their own advantages and disadvantages. Gelatin methacrylate is a photocrosslinked hydrogel obtained by the reaction of gelatin and methacrylic anhydride, which has the characteristics of good biocompatibility, injectability, good drug-carrying performance, controllable drug release rate, and good mechanical properties [ 22 ]. It has been widely used in research fields such as cell 3D culture, cartilage tissue engineering, and bio-3D printing, etc [ [23] , [24] , [25] , [26] , [27] , [28] ]. GelMA is also one of the most used hydrogel materials in the clinic, and its safety is effectively guaranteed, making it an ideal scaffold for cartilage tissue engineering. For example, Miao et al. used GelMA microspheres to treat osteoarthritis and found that they could promote chondrocyte synthesis and metabolism to promote cartilage repair [ 29 ]. Wan et al. used GelMA encapsulated exosomes to target chondrocytes to promote cartilage repair by maintaining their homeostasis [ 30 ]. Liu et al. used to regulate bone marrow mesenchymal stem cell (BMSC) activity by adjusting the viscoelasticity of GelMA hydrogel to promote cartilage repair [ 31 ]. Li et al. utilized GelMA hydrogel microspheres to promote cartilage repair by enhancing the paracrine activity of stem cells [ 32 ]. Therefore, GelMA hydrogels are ideal as slow-release scaffolds loaded with CeO 2 nanoparticles and Urolithin A based on their excellent properties.

In this study, CeUA@GelMA was innovatively constructed for cartilage defect repair by co-loading CeO 2 nanoparticles in GelMA hydrogels with Urolithin A. CeO 2 nanoparticles, through redox cycling in its high valence state (Ce 4+ ) exhibited superoxide dismutase-like and catalase activities for long-lasting scavenging of ROS such as O 2 − , H 2 O 2 , etc. Urolithin A specifically activated the PINK1/Parkin pathway and promoted the phagocytosis of damaged mitochondria by autophagosomes. In in vitro experiments, CeUA@GelMA not only effectively promoted chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs, but also effectively reduced ROS levels and promoted autophagy of damaged mitochondria in BMSCs under oxidative stress. In in vivo experiments, CeUA@GelMA could effectively promote the repair of cartilage defects in rats within six weeks. The core innovation of this study is the construction of a dual-function antioxidant-autophagy activation hydrogel system for the first time, which breaks through the bottleneck of cartilage repair at the level of mitochondrial homeostasis, and provides a new way of thinking for the development of cartilage repair materials.
sections.methods:
CeUA@GelMA was composed of GelMA hydrogel mixed with CeO 2 and Urolithin A. The GelMA hydrogel was prepared by adding 1 g of GelMA (EFL, China) to 20 mL of PBS for 30 min at 60 °C and protected from light. After complete dissolution, lithium phenyl-2,4,6-trimethylbenzoylphosphonate (LAP) (EFL, China), CeO 2 nanoparticles (XFNANO, China), and urolithin A (MERCK, USA) were added to the GelMA solution to form CeUA@GelMA premix (0.25 % LAP, 100 μg/mL CeO 2 nanoparticles, 10 μg/mL Urolithin A). Finally, pour the premix into a standard container, and CeUA@GelMA forms after 30 s under 365 nm UV light and an intensity of 5 mW/cm 2 .

The freeze-dried hydrogel samples were sputter-coated with a thin gold layer employing a high-vacuum ion coater (Leica EM ACE600, Germany). Subsequently, the surface characteristics and microstructural features were examined using a field-emission scanning electron microscope (JSM-7500F, Japan).

The swelling ratio of the hydrogels was determined using the gravimetric method based on a previously established protocol. The initial dry weight (M 0 ) of each hydrogel was recorded. Hydrogels were then immersed in PBS at room temperature to swell, and their swollen weight (M 1 ) was measured. The swelling ratio was calculated as: Swelling ratio= (M1/M0) × 100 %.

Hydrogels were incubated in complete medium at 37 °C. At predetermined time points (7, 14, 21, and 28 days), samples were retrieved, freeze-dried, and weighed (M 1 ). The weight retention ratio was calculated as: Weight retention ratio=(M1/M0) × 100 %.

Rat bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) were procured from a commercial cell repository (Shanghai, China). These cells were maintained in α-minimum essential medium (α-MEM, Gibco, USA) containing 10 % fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco, USA) and 1 % penicillin-streptomycin solution (Gibco, USA), and incubated at 37 °C in a humidified 5 % CO 2 environment. The medium was refreshed every 48 h, and BMSCs at passage 3 were utilized for subsequent experiments.

Four hydrogel precursor solutions (200 μL/well) were cast into a 24-well plate (Nest, China) and photocrosslinked. Prior to use, all precursor solutions were filtered through 0.22 μm membranes. BMSCs were seeded at a density of 1 × 10 4 cells per well and co-cultured with the hydrogels for 1, 3, and 5 days. Cell viability was assessed using a Calcein AM/PI double-staining kit (Beyotime, China). After 30 min of incubation with the staining solution, live and dead cells were visualized using an inverted fluorescence microscope (Olympus CKX3-SLP, Japan). In addition, the hydrogel-cell constructs were stained with Calcein AM/PI and examined by confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM, Olympus FV3000, Japan) following the co-culture period. The ratio of live to dead cells was quantified using ImageJ software. Cell proliferation within the hydrogels was evaluated with a Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8, Beyotime, China). At each time point (days 1, 3, and 5), the CCK-8 reagent was diluted 1:1 with culture medium, added to each well, and incubated at 37 °C under 5 % CO 2 for 2 h. The absorbance at 450 nm was measured using a multifunctional microplate reader (Biotech CTYTATION5, USA).

Cell migration was investigated via a scratch assay. BMSCs were co-cultured with hydrogels until reaching 90 % confluence. A scratch was made using a 200 μL pipette tip, and the pre-crosslinked hydrogel was gently placed directly over the cell-free scratch region to ensure close contact with the cut edges of the monolayer. After 24 h of further co-culture, cell migration was visualized by Calcein AM/PI staining under an inverted fluorescence microscope, and the migration rate was analyzed using ImageJ.

BMSCs were induced to oxidative stress by 100 μM H 2 O 2 for 24 h. The mitochondrial membrane potential of BMSCs was evaluated using the JC-1 fluorescent probe. Following 24-h treatment with GelMA, Ce@GelMA, UA@ GelMA, or CeUA@ GelMA, the cells were incubated with JC-1 (1 mg/L) for 20 min at 37 °C. After PBS washing, fluorescence intensity was quantified via confocal laser scanning microscopy (GE, USA).

Following a 24-h pre-culture period in 35 mm confocal dishes, BMSCs were induced to oxidative stress by 100 μM H 2 O 2 for 24 h. BMSCs were treated with GelMA, Ce@GelMA, UA@ GelMA, or CeUA@ GelMA for an additional 24 h. Subsequent staining procedures involved sequential incubation with 0.1 μM MitoTracker dye (30 min, 37 °C) followed by 0.1 μM LysoTracker dye (30 min, 37 °C). Fluorescence imaging was then performed using confocal microscopy to analyze intensity variations.

Hydrogel precursor solutions (200 μL per well) were photocrosslinked in 24-well plates (Nest, China). BMSCs (1 × 10 4 cells/well) were seeded and cultured in chondrogenic induction medium. The culture medium was supplemented with multiple components including 1 mM sodium pyruvate (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 10 ng/mL TGF-β3 (Meilunbio, China), 50 μM H 2 O 2 , 0.1 μM dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich, USA), 1 % ITS supplement (Oricellbio, China), and 1 μM ascorbic acid-2-phosphate (Sigma-Aldrich, USA). Medium replacement was performed every 48 h. At 7 and 14 days, cellular samples were fixed using 4 % paraformaldehyde solution followed by histological staining with 1 % Alcian blue (pH 2.5) for half an hour. Staining results were imaged using a multifunctional microplate reader. For quantitative analysis, cells were washed with 6M guanidine hydrochloride to elute the dye, and the absorbance of the eluate was measured at 630 nm. At 7 days, cellular samples were fixed using 4 % paraformaldehyde solution followed by histological staining with 1 % 1,9-dimethylmeth ylene blue (DMMB) for 1 min. Staining results were imaged using a multifunctional microplate reader. Based on the absorbance values of the samples, the corresponding sGAG concentrations for each group were obtained from the standard curve. On the 7 day, the cell culture media of each group were collected and centrifuged at 4 °C (10,000× g , 10 min) to remove cell debris and impurities. According to the manufacturer's instructions, the COL II content in each group was detected using the ELISA test kit (ml058801, Mlbio, China). Chondrogenic differentiation-related gene expression, including Sox9, Acan, Col II, Col I, Col X, Parkin, and Pink1, was analyzed using qRT-PCR. Primer sequences are provided in Table 1 . Total RNA from each group was extracted, reverse transcribed into cDNA, and subjected to quantitative PCR. The relative gene expression levels were determined. Six-week-old male SD rats (approximately 150 g) were obtained from Changzhou Cavens Experimental Animal Co., Ltd. All animal procedures adhered to ethical guidelines and were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Shanghai Geriatric Medical Center (Ethical Approval No: B2025017). Rats were randomly divided into four groups: Sham, Control, GelMA and CeUA@GelMA. Under general anesthesia (80 mg/kg sodium pentobarbital), a cartilage defect model (2 mm diameter, 1.5 mm depth) was created in the central region of the femoral trochlear groove. GelMA or CeUA@GelMA were implanted into the defect site and secured with fibrin glue. The joint capsule and skin were sutured and disinfected. Post-surgery, standardized care was provided. At week 4 post-surgery, rats were euthanized, and femurs were collected for preliminary analysis. At week 8, femurs, major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys), and abdominal aortic blood samples were collected for further evaluation. Macroscopic observation of femoral condyle cartilage was performed at weeks 4 and 8 to assess repair outcomes. Femoral samples were fixed in 4 % formalin for 48 h. Surface roughness of the regenerated cartilage was analyzed using atomic force microscopy (AFM, Bruker Dimension Icon, n = 3). Samples were decalcified over 6 weeks, dehydrated through an ethanol gradient, and embedded in paraffin. Sections (10 μm thick) were stained with Safranin O/Fast Green and HE to evaluate cartilage regeneration. Immunohistochemical staining was performed to detect ACAN and Col II expression in the defect area. ImageJ software was used to quantify protein expression levels. To evaluate the biocompatibility of GelMA and CeUA@GelMA as implants, samples from major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys) were collected at week 8 for histological staining. Blood samples from the abdominal aorta were analyzed for routine blood parameters and liver and kidney function. The combined results comprehensively assessed the biocompatibility and repair efficacy of the implants.

To investigate the developmental patterns of BMSCs and CeUA@GelMA during culture, BMSCs from CeUA@GelMA at 2 weeks of culture were collected. Note that during the two-week culture process, we used cartilage induction medium with 50 μM H 2 O 2 added to culture the two groups. Change the culture medium every two days. Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent, and RNA libraries were constructed. High-throughput sequencing was performed by OE Biotech Co., Ltd. (China) to analyze transcriptomic profiles.

Data were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analysis was performed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or t -test using GraphPad Prism 9 software. P < 0.05 was considered to be statistically significant.
sections.results:
In order to investigate the stability of CeUA@GelMA, we first characterized the physicochemical properties of CeUA@GelMA. First, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images ( Fig. 1 B) analysis revealed that the CeO 2 nanoparticles exhibited a generally spherical morphology with a particle size distribution of about 50 nm, indicating good homogeneity in size. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis ( Fig. 1 C) revealed that all lyophilized hydrogels exhibited an interconnected porous architecture, qualitatively suggesting a 3D network that could potentially provide diffusion channels and loading space. It is noted that the observed pore structure is a result of the lyophilization process and serves for qualitative comparison. Fig. 1 Preparation and characterization of CeUA@GelMA. Dynamic rheological analysis showed that the storage modulus (G′) of all hydrogel was stably maintained between 0.1 and 1 KPa in the angular frequency range of 1–100 rad/s ( Fig. 1 D). The loss modulus (G″) of all hydrogels are between 10 −3 and 10 −4 kPa, which conforms to the characteristics of gel-forming ( Fig. 1 E). In addition, steady-state shear experiments ( Fig. 1 F) revealed that the viscosity of the composite hydrogels decreases with increasing shear rate, and the CeUA@GelMA viscosity of 10 3 Pa s at 0.1 s −1 , which is in line with the lubrication requirement of articular cartilage. We also explored the in vitro degradation and swelling behavior of each group of hydrogels. The degradation rate of CeUA@GelMA in 37 °C PBS was significantly lower than that of the pure GelMA group, which offers the possibility of long-term drug release. The swelling experiments ( Fig. 1 H) showed that all groups of hydrogels reached the swelling equilibrium within 30 h, which indicated that the incorporation of CeO 2 and Urolithin A had little effect on the swelling properties of GelMA. Finally, we also explored the drug release rates of CeO 2 and Urolithin A ( Fig. 1 I). Furthermore, we investigated the rheological properties of each hydrogel during swelling and degradation at 28 days ( Fig. 1J–L and M − O), and found that the stored modulus and lost modulus decreased compared with when the hydrogel was just cross-linked. This indicates that with the increase of time, the internal three-dimensional network structure of each hydrogel has relaxed or partially damaged, resulting in a decrease in its mechanical strength. The release rates of CeO 2 and Urolithin A were significantly greater in at the early stage than at the later stage, but both were close to 100 % within 60 days. This also indicates that high concentrations of CeO 2 and Urolithin A in the early stage can rapidly remove excessive ROS and activate mitophagy to remove damaged mitochondria, forming a dynamic regulation mode of “repair first, protect later”.

After completing the exploration of the physicochemical properties of CeUA@GelMA, the present study evaluated the biocompatibility of CeUA@GelMA composite hydrogels by a multidimensional experimental system to ensure that they could function effectively and safely in vivo . First, live/dead staining analysis ( Fig. 2 A) showed that the survival rate of BMSCs was higher than 99 % (green fluorescence) and there were no dead cells (red fluorescence) in all groups of hydrogels versus Control, confirming the material-based biosafety. Cytotoxicity was further quantified by the CCK-8 method ( Fig. 2 C), and the absorbance value of CeUA@GelMA group was not significantly different from that of the pure GelMA group after 5 days of incubation, which indicated that the incorporation of CeO 2 and Urolithin A did not affect the biocompatibility of GelMA. The cell proliferation assay ( Fig. 2 D) further revealed that BMSCs were able to proliferate normally in all groups of hydrogels. In terms of cell migration behavior ( Fig. 2 B and E), CeUA@GelMA demonstrated unique regulatory advantages. Scratch experiments showed that the migration rate of the CeUA@GelMA group reached 70 % at 24 h, which was significantly higher than that of the pure GelMA group and the CeO 2 @GelMA and UA@GelMA groups. In conclusion, CeUA@GelMA has the advantage of multi-level biocompatibility, which provides a key guarantee for it to realize matrix regeneration in cartilage defect repair. After successfully demonstrating the long-term cell culture potential of CeUA@GelMA, we evaluated an important function of CeUA@GelMA namely the ability to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis. As the center of energy metabolism in eukaryotic cells, mitochondria have an oxidative phosphorylation reaction that is the core mechanism of ATP biosynthesis. During this process, there is by-product generation of electron transfer reactions in the electron transport chain (ETC), where a small amount of incompletely reduced electrons combine with oxygen molecules to form superoxide anion O 2 − , and the physiological concentration of this type of ROS is dynamically regulated by the intracellular enzymatic antioxidant defense system. When metabolic imbalance is triggered by mitochondrial defects in the ETC complex or external damaging factors, the rate of ROS generation significantly exceeds the antioxidant scavenging capacity, resulting in the disruption of redox homeostasis [ 33 , 34 ]. The mitochondrial transmembrane potential (ΔΨm), an important indicator of mitochondrial function, is dependent on the proton gradient established by the ETC proton pump, an electrochemical potential that is necessary for ATP synthase to catalyze the phosphorylation of ADP, and a sustained decrease in ΔΨm is often indicative of disturbed mitochondrial energy metabolism [ [35] , [36] , [37] ]. Therefore, we assessed the mitochondrial status of cells by detecting ROS generation, mitochondrial membrane potential, and mitophagy processes. In the present study, we systematically elucidated the core mechanism of CeUA@GelMA composite hydrogel to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis through the dual function of antioxidant-autophagy activation. First, the DCFH-DA fluorescent probe assay ( Fig. 3 A) showed that in the H 2 O 2 induced oxidative stress model, the ROS levels of BMSCs in the CeUA@GelMA and CeO2@GelMA groups were significantly reduced compared with those in the Control group and other hydrogel groups. It was further verified by in vitro free radical scavenging experiments that the scavenging rate of DPPH and OH − was significantly higher in CeUA@GelMA than in GelMA group, and this efficient antioxidant property originated from the redox cycle of CeO 2 nanoparticles ( Fig. 3 B and C). (∗: compared to value at Control groups, # : compared to value at GelMA groups.)

Our JC-1 staining assay using ΔΨm detection further revealed that CeUA@GelMA significantly maintained mitochondrial energy metabolism homeostasis ( Fig. 4 A). Under oxidative stress conditions, the red/green fluorescence ratio of the CeUA@GelMA group was close to that of the normal control group and significantly higher than that of the control group. Key autophagy regulation experiments ( Fig. 4 B) showed that CeUA@GelMA significantly enhanced mitochondrial autophagic flux. By LysoTracker (red) and MitoTracker (green) co-localization analysis, the mitochondria-lysosome co-localization rate in the CeUA@GelMA group was significantly higher than that in the Control group, which indicated that the cells in the CeUA@GelMA group were actively undergoing mitophagy behavior. These results confirmed that the CeUA@GelMA group blocked the abnormal opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore by scavenging ROS, while urolithin A activated mitophagy, and both of them synergistically maintained the stability of ΔΨm, preventing mitochondrial homeostasis disruption. This defense-clearance-repair cascade not only ensures the survival of chondrocytes in the pathological microenvironment, but also promotes the synthesis and remodeling of extracellular matrix by maintaining the balance between mitochondrial biogenesis and autophagy, which lays a molecular foundation for the functional regeneration of cartilage defects. (B) Mitophagy staining results of BMSCs in hydrogels of each group of GelMA, CeO 2 @GelMA, UA@GelMA and CeUA@GelMA. Fig. 4

After systematically comparing the efficacy of each group of hydrogels in regulating the functional homeostasis of mitochondria, the present study further investigated their role in regulating the chondrogenic directed differentiation of BMSCs. Based on the preliminary biosafety validation, a two-week chondrogenic induction culture was performed on BMSCs. Spatio-temporal distribution analysis of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) by chondroitin sulfate-specific staining showed ( Fig. 5 A and B) that compared with the blank control group, the GelMA and CeO 2 @GelMA group, UA@GelMA group, and CeUA@GelMA group all showed more significant enhancement of heterostaining in the mid-to late-phase culture stages, with the CeUA@ GelMA composite hydrogel group exhibited the most significant enrichment of staining signals at the terminal stage (14 days), suggesting an optimal cartilage matrix-induced synthesis. This biological effect may be closely related to the fact that the composite hydrogel improves the functional state of mitochondria by regulating the redox balance, thus maintaining the microenvironment for the proliferation and differentiation of BMSCs. (B) Quantitative analysis of Alisin blue staining. (C) Relative GAG content of BMSCs co-cultured with GelMA, CeO2@GelMA, UA@GelMA and CeUA@GelMA at day 7. To further investigate the effects of different hydrogels on the chondrogenic differentiation of BMSCs, the GAG and type II collagen (Col II) contents in the hydrogels were quantitatively assessed using the 1,9-dimethylmeth ylene blue (DMMB) assay and enzyme-linked immuno sorbent assay (ELISA) ( Fig. 5 C and D). The experimental data showed that the CeUA@GelMA co-culture system exhibited statistically significant differences in collagen type II (Col II) and GAG content on day 7 compared with the single-function modification groups (CeO2@GelMA, UA@GelMA) and the base material group (GelMA), confirming the positive regulatory effect of functional synergistic effects on the key factors of cartilage formation. The cartilage-related gene expression profiles were further systematically assessed by quantitative PCR technique ( Fig. 5 E–I). The results showed that the CeUA@GelMA group significantly up-regulated the transcript levels of the core regulators of cartilage phenotype (Col II, Sox9, ACAN), while effectively suppressing the expression bias of fibrosis-related genes (Col I) and hypertrophic character genes (Col X). In particular, the mRNA abundance of Col II and ACAN was significantly elevated compared with other experimental groups, confirming that the composite hydrogel could effectively promote the synthesis of cartilage-specific markers. These results demonstrated the cartilage differentiation potential of the CeUA@GelMA group, highlighting its unique advantage in remodeling the cartilage regeneration microenvironment.

To further investigate the biological effects of CeUA@GelMA hydrogels on BMSCs under oxidative stress, we performed mRNA-seq analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) ( Fig. 6 A) revealed that the gene expression profiles of Control and CeUA@GelMA groups showed significant separation in the first principal component (PC1) and second principal component (PC2), indicating that the material treatment significantly altered the global transcriptional state of the cells. Differential gene analysis further revealed that there were a total of 208 significantly up-regulated and 327 down-regulated genes in the CeUA@GelMA group ( Fig. 6 B). The volcano plot ( Fig. 6 C) showed that the up-regulated genes were mainly enriched in ECM synthesis-related pathways, while the down-regulated genes were concentrated in inflammatory responses and fibrosis markers, suggesting that CeUA@GelMA reshaped the functional cellular phenotypes through bidirectional regulation. Gene expression clustering heatmap ( Fig. 6 E) showed that the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in the CeUA@GelMA group formed two characteristic modules: Module I contained key regulators of mitophagy (PINK1, Parkin) and antioxidant enzymes (SOD2, GPX4), whose expression levels were elevated compared with that of control group; while Module II encompassed the ECM-degrading enzymes (MMP13, ADAMTS5) and pro-inflammatory factors (NFKB1, STAT3) with decreased expression. The hierarchical clustering of expression patterns further confirmed the synergistic regulation of redox homeostasis and matrix homeostasis by the materials, and the GO enrichment analysis ( Fig. 6 D) showed that the up-regulated genes in the CeUA@GelMA group were significantly enriched in the “Organelle organization”, “Cell cycle process” and “Extracellular matrix”. Notably, the expression of genes related to “Microtubule cytoskeleton organization” and “Chromosome organization” was up-regulated, suggesting that the material safeguards the mitochondrial function by maintaining the mitochondria. KEGG pathway analysis ( Fig. 6 F) further revealed that the differential genes were mainly enriched in the “ECM-receptor interaction”, “Pink1-Parkin signaling pathway” and “ECM-receptor interaction”, and “PI3K-Akt signaling pathway”. Among them, the up-regulation of integrin and laminin genes in the ECM pathway was consistent with the function of the material in promoting cartilage matrix deposition. In addition, the KEGG results also predicted that CeUA@GelMA may promote mitophagy in BMSCs through the Pink1-Parkin pathway. We also used PCR experiments to detect the expression of Pink1 and parkin genes in the CeUA@GelMA group on the fourteenth day ( Fig. 6 G and H). The results proved that CeUA@GelMA promoted the expression of Pink1 and parkin in BMSCs under oxidative stress. Fig. 6 Transcriptomic analysis. In order to systematically evaluate the cartilage regeneration efficacy of CeUA@GelMA composites, a rat knee joint whole-layer cartilage defect model was constructed in this study (defect size: 2 × 1.5 mm). The experimental animals were randomly divided into four groups: the sham operation group (only the articular surface was exposed), the blank control group (the defect was untreated), the GelMA-filled group and the CeUA@GelMA treatment group. Femoral condyles and major organs specimens were collected at 4 and 8 weeks postoperatively for multidimensional evaluation, respectively. The gross morphological analysis revealed ( Fig. 7 A) that the CeUA@GelMA group showed hyaline-like cartilage-like repair tissue at 4 weeks, and its surface flatness was similar to that of the sham-operated group; whereas the control group and the GelMA group still had obvious fibrous repair and poor interface integration at 8 weeks. Quantitative analysis using the International Cartilage Repair Society (ICRS) scoring system showed ( Fig. 7 B) that the CeUA@GelMA group had a significantly higher repair quality score at 6 weeks compared with the other intervention groups, confirming its unique advantage of accelerating cartilage structural remodeling. The surface topology of the repaired tissues was further analyzed using nanoscale characterization techniques ( Fig. 7 C and D). Atomic force microscopy examination showed that the average surface roughness (Ra value) at 8 weeks in the CeUA@GelMA group was not statistically different from that of the sham-operated group (P > 0.05), whereas the Ra values of the control group and the GelMA group were significantly increased. Micro-morphological observation showed that the collagen fibers in the CeUA@GelMA group showed a highly ordered reticular arrangement, and their three-dimensional topology was highly similar to that of the natural cartilage matrix, which was closely related to their excellent mechanical integration properties. Fig. 7 (A) Macroscopic images of cartilage tissue in the distal femur after 4W and 8W of treatment. (B) Heat map of ICRS score of cartilage at 4W and 8W of treatment. (C) AFM image of the regenerated area of cartilage surface after 8W of treatment. (D) Roughness parameter of the regenerated area of cartilage surface after 8W of treatment. (∗: compared to value at Sham groups, # : compared to value at Control groups.) Fig. 7

In the present study, we used Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE) staining to reveal the microstructural features of the tissue ( Fig. 8 A), and the results showed that the CeUA@GelMA group formed hyaline cartilage-like structures at 4 weeks postoperatively, and its characteristic chondrocyte arrangement pattern was highly compatible with that of the Sham group, and there was no cartilage fibrosis signs or inflammatory infiltration with the prolongation of the repair time (up to 8 weeks). In contrast, the control and GelMA groups showed matrix dissociation at the early stage (4 weeks), and immature repair features such as regional collagen disorganization were still present at the late stage (8 weeks). Matrix maturation was quantitatively assessed by Safranin and Fast Green staining ( Fig. 8 B), and it was found that the density of chondroitin total sulfate deposition in the CeUA@GelMA group was similar to that of Sham at 4 weeks, and the intensity of the heterostaining was not statistically different from that of natural cartilage by 8 weeks (P > 0.05), which was significantly superior to that of the control group and the GelMA group. These results demonstrated that the CeUA@GelMA group exhibited a repair effect close to that of natural cartilage in terms of both tissue structure and matrix composition. Based on immunohistochemical localization analysis, this study systematically resolved the reconstruction characteristics of cartilage-specific matrix. Regarding the spatial distribution of type II collagen, the CeUA@GelMA group exhibited a continuous and homogenized positive signal gradient band at 4 weeks postoperatively, with its integrated optical density per unit area value was not significantly different from that of the Sham group ( Fig. 9 A and C). In contrast, both the Control and GelMA groups showed discrete patches of positive signal at successive time points, suggesting a severe delay in collagen network reconstruction. The dynamic evolution pattern of aggregated proteoglycans further revealed the maturity of matrix function ( Fig. 9 B and D). A gradient expression pattern similar to that of natural cartilage was established in the CeUA@GelMA group at an early stage (4 weeks), and the area of positively stained areas was significantly better than that of the Control and GelMA groups. By the late stage of repair (8 weeks), the difference between the proteoglycan deposition density of this group and that of the Sham group was greatly reduced, whereas significant heterogeneous expression remained in the Control group. To comprehensively assess the long-term safety of the material, systematic biosafety was verified by multi-organ pathology analysis ( Fig. S1 ) and dynamic monitoring of metabolic indicators ( Fig. S2 ). Observations across multiple time points showed that no abnormal histologic changes were observed in the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys and other parenchymal organs of the experimental animals in the CeUA@GelMA group, and their liver enzyme profiles and renal function indexes were consistently maintained within physiological fluctuating intervals (P > 0.05). These data, ranging from molecular deposition patterns to systemic toxicity, confirm that CeUA@GelMA has both excellent cartilage biomimetic repair ability and reliable biomedical material safety characteristics. sections.conclusion:
The choice of GelMA as the scaffold material in this study was based on its well-suited properties for cartilage tissue engineering. Compared to other natural hydrogels, GelMA offers inherent bioactivity, including cell-adhesive motifs and enzyme-degradable sites that facilitate cell migration and tissue remodeling. Furthermore, unlike some synthetic hydrogels, GelMA provides a naturally derived microenvironment that is more conducive to chondrogenesis. However, a recognized limitation of GelMA, and many hydrogels in general, is its mechanical strength, which is typically lower than that of native cartilage tissue. While GelMA presents certain limitations, its advantages in terms of biocompatibility, tunability, and support for chondrocyte phenotype make it a scaffold material for investigating the fundamental mechanisms of cartilage repair. GelMA hydrogel, as an excellent drug delivery platform, demonstrates great potential for loading bioactive macromolecules such as exosomes or growth factors. However, its application is accompanied by inherent challenges. Its advantages lie in: GelMA's 3D network structure can effectively encapsulate and protect exosomes or growth factors from enzymatic degradation, offering excellent biocompatibility and cell infiltration; its photocrosslinking enables a mild drug-loading process and the creation of complex biomimetic structures; more importantly, the degradation rate of GelMA can be modulated to achieve sustained and controlled release of therapeutic molecules. Nevertheless, its significant limitations include: exosomes face challenges such as difficulties in isolation and purification, low yield, batch-to-batch variability, and limited drug loading efficiency; growth factors suffer from an extremely short in vivo half-life, poor stability, susceptibility to inactivation, high production costs, and the risk of potential off-target effects. Therefore, in this study, the use of GelMA loading to easily prepare CeO 2 and Urolithin A with good stability and high half-life is an effective strategy for treating cartilage defects.

The core challenge in cartilage repair lies in the vicious cycle triggered by mitochondrial dysfunction in the pathological microenvironment excessive ROS accumulation leads to oxidative stress, while insufficient autophagic capacity further exacerbates the retention of damaged mitochondria. This study constructed a defense-clearance-repair cascade regulation system by integrating CeO 2 nanoparticles and urolithin A. TEM and rheological analysis confirmed that CeO 2 nanoparticles were uniformly distributed within the GelMA network, and their mixed-valence redox cycling endowed the material with long-lasting ROS scavenging capacity. Transcriptomic data further revealed that CeUA@GelMA significantly upregulated mitophagy-related genes and antioxidant enzymes, while suppressing inflammatory cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes. This dual regulatory effect effectively disrupts the oxidative stress-mitochondrial damage-inflammatory amplification pathological triad, providing BMSCs with a stable differentiation microenvironment. Compared to single antioxidant strategies, this dual-functional design not only addresses the short half-life and poor penetration of traditional antioxidants but also actively clears damaged mitochondria via autophagy activation, thereby rebuilding mitochondrial homeostasis at the molecular level.

Multi-level experiments from in vitro to in vivo showed that the promotive effect of CeUA@GelMA on cartilage regeneration stems from its multi-dimensional regulation of cell behavior and matrix synthesis. At the cellular level, the material safeguarded the homeostasis and viability of BMSCs by maintaining ΔΨm stability and enhancing mitochondrial autophagic flux. Meanwhile, CeUA@GelMA directed BMSCs toward chondrogenic phenotypic differentiation by activating the Sox9-ACAN-Col II signaling axis and inhibiting the expression of fibrosis (Col I) and hypertrophy (Col X) markers. This differentiation-regulating ability may be closely related to its improved mitochondrial biosynthesis and ECM receptor interactions. At the tissue level, AFM and histological analyses revealed that CeUA@GelMA-mediated repair tissues had a surface topology and matrix composition gradient highly similar to that of natural cartilage. This bionic property originated from the slow release modulation of CeO 2 and UA by GelMA hydrogel, which enabled the rapid clearance of ROS and activation of autophagy by high drug concentration in the early stage, while the sustained release in the later stage maintained the repair microenvironment and formed a dynamic balance. Compared with single GelMA or functionalized modification group, the synergistic effect of CeUA@GelMA shows significant advantages in ICRS score, collagen arrangement and proteoglycan deposition density.

While our in vitro data demonstrate the efficacy of CeO 2 and Urolithin A in protecting chondrocytes under inflammatory stress, several translational considerations must be addressed. Firstly, ROS play a nuanced role in cartilage homeostasis, involved not only in pathology but also in adaptive responses and hypoxic signaling. Our treatment strategy aims to scavenge pathological excess ROS while theoretically preserving physiological ROS signaling, a balance that requires further investigation in more complex models. Secondly, the avascular nature of cartilage presents a significant challenge for drug delivery, likely resulting in steep concentration gradients and transient exposure in vivo . To overcome this, future studies will employ localized, sustained-release delivery systems and detailed pharmacokinetic analyses to ensure that therapeutic concentrations are maintained within the joint space and cartilage tissue over a clinically relevant duration. Addressing these aspects will be crucial for the successful translation of this combinatory therapy.

Despite the significant repair results achieved in animal models in this study, several key issues still need to be addressed for the clinical application of CeUA@GelMA. First, the long-term biosafety of the material needs to be further verified. Although no signs of toxicity were found in multi-organ pathology and liver and kidney function tests, the potential bioaccumulation effects of CeO 2 nanoparticles and their long-term effects on the immune system still need to be evaluated by experiments with larger sample sizes and longer observation periods. In animal experiments, this study also used the minimum sample size for exploration. In the future, the sample size will be expanded to prove the efficacy of CeUA@GelMA. Furthermore, cartilage differentiation is a dynamic process. This study only focused on the situation of cartilage differentiation on the 7 days. In future studies, we will pay more attention to the situation of cartilage differentiation within 28 days to comprehensively explore the mechanism by which CeUA@GelMA promotes cartilage differentiation. This study only utilized PCR and sequencing results to demonstrate that CeUA@GelMA can promote the Pink1-Parkin pathway of BMSCs under oxidative stress. Subsequently, this study will design experiments on the expression of mitochondrial autophagy proteins to further prove the ability of CeUA@GelMA to maintain mitochondrial homeostasis. Finally, in-depth analysis of the material-cell interaction mechanism will promote the optimization of its function. For example, revealing the differences in the response of BMSCs subpopulations to CeUA@GelMA by single-cell sequencing or simulating the repair process in pathological microenvironments by using organoid models can provide more comprehensive theoretical support for clinical translation. In this study, we successfully constructed a CeUA@GelMA hydrogel with both ROS scavenging and mitophagy activation functions, which significantly promoted cartilage regeneration through a multi-scale regulatory mechanism. From the reconstruction of mitochondrial homeostasis at the molecular level, to the deposition of biomimetic matrix at the tissue level, to the validation of biosafety at the system level, the results of the study will provide innovative ideas for the development of the next-generation cartilage repair materials.
